claim: During cytokinesis in Caenorhabditis elegans, the per-unit-length constriction rate increases as ring perimeter decreases.
source: Thus, the per-unit-length constriction rate increases as ring perimeter decreases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key observation that motivates the study.

claim: The per-unit-length amount of ring components (myosin, anillin) increases with exponential kinetics during constriction.
source: We found that, per unit length, the amount of ring components (myosin, anillin) and the constriction rate increase with parallel exponential kinetics.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The per-unit-length constriction rate increases with exponential kinetics during ring closure.
source: We found that, per unit length, the amount of ring components (myosin, anillin) and the constriction rate increase with parallel exponential kinetics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3C.

claim: The cortex within the ring is compressed along the axis perpendicular to the ring during constriction.
source: Quantitative analysis of cortical flow indicated that the cortex within the ring is compressed along the axis perpendicular to the ring, and the per-unit-length rate of cortical compression increases during constriction in proportion to ring myosin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cortical flow analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The per-unit-length rate of cortical compression increases during constriction in proportion to ring myosin.
source: Quantitative analysis of cortical flow indicated that the cortex within the ring is compressed along the axis perpendicular to the ring, and the per-unit-length rate of cortical compression increases during constriction in proportion to ring myosin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3C showing parallel exponential kinetics.

claim: Positive feedback between ring myosin and compression-driven flow of cortex into the ring drives an exponential increase in the per-unit-length amount of ring myosin.
source: We propose that positive feedback between ring myosin and compression-driven flow of cortex into the ring drives an exponential increase in the per-unit-length amount of ring myosin to maintain a high ring constriction rate and support this proposal with an analytical mathematical model.
evidence: This is the main proposal of the paper stated in the abstract and supported by mathematical modeling in Figure 4.

claim: The surface area of the cell increases by approximately 40% during the first division of the C. elegans embryo.
source: During the first division of the C. elegans embryo, the surface area of the cell increases by ~40% to accommodate the shape change that generates the daughter cells.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative observation in the Results section.

claim: Cortical surface at the cell poles expands in response to tension generated by the constricting ring.
source: The cortical velocity profile measured from the flow map indicated that the cortical surface at the cell poles expands as the ring constricts, whereas the cortex in the region between the poles and the division plane flows at constant velocity towards the division plane, without expansion or compression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the flow map analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The cortex in the region between the poles and the division plane flows at constant velocity towards the division plane without expansion or compression.
source: The cortical velocity profile measured from the flow map indicated that the cortical surface at the cell poles expands as the ring constricts, whereas the cortex in the region between the poles and the division plane flows at constant velocity towards the division plane, without expansion or compression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Cortical tension does not impose significant resistance to ring pulling during cytokinesis.
source: In contrast, the measured constriction rate was not increased after cutting (0.18 ± 0.03 µm/s; Figure 2B,C), indicating that cortical tension does not impose significant resistance to ring pulling.
evidence: This is concluded from laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inhibiting the Arp2/3 complex by depleting ARX-2 does not alter the constriction rate.
source: Consistent with the results of the laser cutting experiments, inhibiting the Arp2/3 complex by depleting its ARX-2 subunit, which is expected to reduce effective cortical viscosity and thus cortical tension (Chaudhuri et al., 2007; Davies et al., 2014; Tseng and Wirtz, 2004), also did not alter the constriction rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, with citations to prior work on Arp2/3 effects on cortical viscosity.

claim: The constriction rate is limited by ring-internal friction rather than cortical tension.
source: The fact that cortical tension does not limit the rate of ring constriction suggests that the constriction rate is instead limited by ring-internal friction.
evidence: This is inferred from the laser ablation and Arp2/3 inhibition experiments.

claim: Ring myosin generated force primarily counters ring internal friction to drive ring constriction.
source: We conclude that the viscosity of the polar cortex is negligible compared to the viscosity internal to the ring; thus, ring myosin generated force primarily counters ring internal friction to drive ring constriction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The equatorial cortex is uniformly compressed across a 10 µm wide region along the perpendicular-to-the-ring axis during contractile ring assembly.
source: The linear gradient indicated that, during contractile ring assembly, when the ring is on the embryo surface, cortical surface is uniformly compressed across a 10 µm wide region along the perpendicular-to-the-ring axis between the two relaxing poles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the flow map at early time points shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cortical surface area compression within the Rho zone/contractile ring continues during ring constriction.
source: This result suggests that cortical surface area compression along the axis perpendicular to the ring persists throughout constriction.
evidence: This is concluded from analysis of cortical flow into the division plane shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The cortical surface area entering the division plane during ring constriction is significantly greater than the area of the division plane.
source: This analysis revealed that the area of the cortical surface that entered the division plane during ring constriction was significantly greater than the area of the division plane (Figure 3B, middle panel).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The flux of cortical area into the division plane is 1.5- to 2-fold higher than the rate of change in the area of the division plane throughout cytokinesis.
source: The flux of cortical area into the division plane was 1.5- to 2-fold higher than the rate of change in the area of the division plane throughout cytokinesis, suggesting that cortical surface area is continuously compressed within the Rho zone/contractile ring throughout constriction (Figure 3B, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: New cortical surface is pulled into the ring due to cortical compression at a rate proportional to the amount of ring myosin.
source: Thus, new cortical surface is pulled into the ring due to cortical compression at a rate proportional to the amount of ring myosin.
evidence: This is concluded from the parallel exponential kinetics of myosin accumulation and cortical compression shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The per-unit-length constriction rate increases in proportion to the per-unit-length amount of myosin.
source: Like the rate of cortical compression along the perpendicular-to-the-ring axis, the per-unit-length constriction rate also increased in proportion to the per-unit-length amount of myosin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The exponential increase in the per-unit-length constriction rate explains the observed ability of the contractile ring to close at a relatively constant rate despite its progressively decreasing perimeter.
source: The exponential increase in the per-unit-length constriction rate explains the observed ability of the contractile ring to close at a relatively constant rate despite its progressively decreasing perimeter (Bourdages et al., 2014; Carvalho et al., 2009; Zumdieck et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work documenting constant closure rates.

claim: The Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model consists of three equations with three model parameters and can recapitulate the experimentally observed dynamics of ring components, cortical flow into the division plane, and ring constriction.
source: Our model, which we call the Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model, adds compression feedback along the axis perpendicular to the ring into this framework (Figure 4A,B). Our model consists of three equations with three model parameters and can recapitulate the experimentally observed dynamics of ring components, cortical flow into the division plane, and ring constriction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and the model is presented in Figure 4.

claim: In the Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model, myosin in the Rho zone compresses cortical surface, which pulls naive cortex into the Rho zone that is then loaded with myosin and other contractile ring components.
source: We propose that, due to polar relaxation, compression of cortex in the Rho zone pulls naive cortex, defined as cortex outside the Rho zone (naive to RhoA-based signaling) into the Rho zone (Figure 4A). The new cortex that flows into the Rho zone as a result of compression is also loaded with contractile ring components and initiates compression. Thus, along the perpendicular-to-the-ring axis a feedback loop operates in which myosin in the Rho zone compresses cortical surface, which pulls naive surface into the Rho zone that is then loaded with myosin and other contractile ring components, leading to the exponential accumulation of ring components (Figure 4A, left panel).
evidence: This is the core mechanism proposed in the model, stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: In the around-the-ring direction, ring shortening is coupled to the disassembly of ring components and does not change per-unit-length component levels.
source: In the around-the-ring direction, ring shortening is coupled to the disassembly of ring components as we described previously (Constriction-Coupled Disassembly; Carvalho et al., 2009) and does not change per-unit-length component levels (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Division plane photobleaching experiments at the one-cell stage are consistent with the Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model.
source: In summary, our division plane photobleaching experiment at the one-cell stage is consistent with the Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model.
evidence: This is concluded from the photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Bleached myosin subunits are lost in proportion to the reduction in ring perimeter as the ring constricts.
source: From this, we conclude that the bleached subunits are not retained but are lost in proportion to the reduction in ring perimeter as the ring constricts as expected for the Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model (Figure 6B, lower panels).
evidence: This is concluded from the photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The exponential increase in the per-unit-length amount of ring myosin is due to addition of new myosin to the ring.
source: Thus, since the per-unit-length amount of myosin in the ring increases exponentially as the ring closes, this exponential increase must be due to addition of new myosin to the ring.
evidence: This is concluded from the photobleaching experiments showing that bleached myosin is lost while total myosin increases.

claim: There is very little exchange of bleached myosin subunits with fluorescent myosin from the cytoplasm.
source: The fact that fluorescent myosin is added to bleached rings at the same rate as it is added to control rings suggests that there is very little exchange of the bleached myosin subunits with fluorescent myosin from the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from the photobleaching data showing parallel recovery rates.

claim: New myosin appears in bleached four-cell stage arcs in a fashion very similar to bleached rings at the one-cell stage.
source: New myosin appeared in the bleached four-cell stage arcs in a fashion very similar to the bleached rings at the one-cell stage, suggesting that a similar mechanism delivers new myosin into the ring to drive the increase in the per-unit-length constriction rate at the one- and four-cell stages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on photobleaching experiments at the four-cell stage shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The polar cortex has unique mechanical properties compared to the intervening cortex that does not expand.
source: The differential response of the polar cortex to ring-generated tension is consistent with the idea of polar relaxation hypothesized in early conceptual models of cytokinesis (Greenspan, 1978; Swann and Mitchison, 1958; Taber, 1995; White and Borisy, 1983; Wolpert, 1960; Zinemanas and Nir, 1987, 1988), and suggests that the polar cortex has unique mechanical properties compared to the intervening cortex that does not expand (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expansion behavior and cited in relation to prior conceptual models.

claim: The viscosity of the polar cortex is negligible compared to the viscosity internal to the ring.
source: We conclude that the viscosity of the polar cortex is negligible compared to the viscosity internal to the ring; thus, ring myosin generated force primarily counters ring internal friction to drive ring constriction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is concluded from the laser ablation and Arp2/3 inhibition experiments.

claim: Ring constriction drives expansion of the polar cortex.
source: Ring constriction, in turn, affects cortical tension and drives expansion of the polar cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the flow map and laser ablation experiments.

claim: The per-unit-length increase in the concentration of myosin and other contractile ring components underlies the acceleration of the constriction rate.
source: This finding suggests that the per-unit-length increase in the concentration of myosin and other contractile ring components underlies the acceleration of the constriction rate, and argues against the contractile unit model, which we had previously proposed to explain how the per-unit-length constriction rate might increase in the absence of a proportional increase in component levels (Carvalho et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data showing exponential accumulation of components.

claim: The overall amounts of myosin and anillin in the ring remain relatively constant as the ring constricts.
source: In this model, the overall amounts of myosin, anillin (and presumably other components) in the ring would remain relatively constant as the ring constricts, as is experimentally observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), due to a balance between loss resulting from disassembly-coupled ring shortening and accumulation due to the feedback loop in the perpendicular-to-the-ring direction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relatively constant overall levels of ring components mask a dramatic restructuring of the ring that is occurring during closure.
source: Thus, the relatively constant overall levels of ring components would mask a dramatic restructuring of the ring that is occurring during closure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an implication of the model.

claim: A second advantage of the feedback-based mechanism is that it would render the ring robust to internal or external mechanical challenges.
source: In addition to maintaining a high overall constriction rate to facilitate timely cell content partitioning, a second advantage of the feedback-based mechanism that we propose is that it would render the ring robust to internal or external mechanical challenges, such as cell-cell contacts, obstacles in the crowded cell interior, or defects in the cytokinesis machinery.
evidence: This is proposed in the Discussion section as a potential advantage of the mechanism.

claim: If the ring stalled due to mechanical challenges, the feedback loop would lead to progressive build-up of contractile ring components until the obstacle could be overcome.
source: If the ring stalled due to any of these causes, the feedback loop between ring myosin and compression-based flow along the direction perpendicular to constriction would lead to the progressive build-up of contractile ring components until they reached a level where the obstacle could be overcome and constriction would again be able to proceed.
evidence: This is proposed in the Discussion section as a consequence of the feedback mechanism.

claim: Ring-directed cortical flows similar to those documented in C. elegans have been observed in the context of wound healing.
source: We note that ring-directed cortical flows similar to the ones we document here have also been observed in the context of wound healing (Mandato and Bement, 2003), where they could potentially serve a similar function in allowing the cell to ramp up contractile force and achieve wound closure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior work on wound healing.

claim: Compression of cortical surface within the ring along the direction perpendicular to the ring is consistent with work in S. pombe showing that contractile ring assembly occurs via acto-myosin based compression of an equatorial band of nodes.
source: We note that compression within the ring along the direction perpendicular to the ring is also consistent with work in S. pombe, which has shown that contractile ring assembly occurs via a similar acto-myosin based compression of an equatorial band of nodes into a compact ring along the long axis of the cell (Vavylonis et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to prior work in S. pombe.

claim: In animal cells, the accumulation of ring components due to compression along the direction perpendicular to the ring is ongoing and serves to accelerate the per-unit-length constriction rate as the ring closes.
source: However, in contrast to S. pombe where ring assembly and constriction occur in distinct phases, our model predicts that in animal cells, the accumulation of ring components due to compression along the direction perpendicular to the ring is ongoing and serves to accelerate the per-unit-length constriction rate as the ring closes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a prediction of the model that distinguishes animal cells from S. pombe.

claim: The polar cortex could be less stiff than the rest of the cortex, causing it to stretch and thin in response to ring constriction-induced tension.
source: One possibility is that the polar cortex is less stiff than the rest of the cortex, causing it to stretch and thin in response to ring constriction-induced tension.
evidence: This is proposed in the Discussion section as one possible explanation for polar cortex expansion.

claim: The polar cortex could turnover more rapidly, leading to a higher rate of surface renewal after stretching.
source: Alternatively, the polar cortex could turnover more rapidly, leading to a higher rate of surface renewal after stretching.
evidence: This is proposed in the Discussion section as an alternative explanation for polar cortex expansion.

claim: The polar cortex could be more prone to rupture, repair of which would locally increase cortical surface.
source: A third possibility is that the polar cortex is more prone to rupture, repair of which would locally increase cortical surface.
evidence: This is proposed in the Discussion section as another possible explanation for polar cortex expansion.

claim: Blebs have been reported at the cell poles in cultured vertebrate and Drosophila cells, where they have been proposed to release tension at the poles.
source: Consistent with this last idea, blebs have been reported at the cell poles in cultured vertebrate and Drosophila cells, where they have been proposed to release tension at the poles (Hickson et al., 2006; Sedzinski et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to prior work.

claim: Aurora A, localized to astral microtubules by association with its activator TPXL-1, actively clears contractile ring proteins from the polar cortex in C. elegans.
source: Work in C. elegans has demonstrated the existence of a mechanism in which Aurora A, localized to astral microtubules by association with its activator TPXL-1, actively clears contractile ring proteins from the polar cortex (Mangal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to recent work.

claim: A reduction in f-actin intensity at the cell poles due to delivery of a phosphatase by segregating chromosomes has been reported in Drosophila cells.
source: A reduction in f-actin intensity at the cell poles due to delivery of a phosphatase by segregating chromosomes has also been reported in Drosophila cells (Rodrigues et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior work.

claim: Cleaving sea urchin embryos exhibit constriction kinetics essentially identical to those during the first division of the C. elegans embryo.
source: Cleaving sea urchin embryos exhibit constriction kinetics essentially identical to those during the first division of the C. elegans embryo (Mabuchi, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to prior work.

claim: Sea urchin embryos exhibit a wave of cortical expansion that initiates at the poles and propagates through to the region adjacent to the furrow during ring constriction.
source: Pioneering work measuring the distance between surface-adhered particles and the behavior of pigmented cortex-associated granules (Dan, 1954; Dan and Dan, 1940; Dan et al., 1938), indicated that sea urchin embryos also exhibit a similar pattern of cortical expansion during ring constriction, in this case, a wave of cortical expansion that initiates at the poles and propagates through to the region adjacent to the furrow (Dan et al., 1938; Dan and Ono, 1954; Dan et al., 1937; Gudejko et al., 2012; Swann and Mitchison, 1958).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to classic work by Dan and colleagues.

claim: Monitoring of fluorescent latex spheres, injected stabilized fluorescent actin filaments, and fluorescently labeled myosin II in vertebrate cells revealed concerted cortical flow towards the division plane in the equatorial region that contrasted with random surface movements at the cell poles.
source: Cortical compression and expansion have not been mapped in vertebrate cells; however, monitoring of fluorescent latex spheres adhered to cell surface proteins (Fishkind et al., 1996; Wang et al., 1994), injected stabilized fluorescent actin filaments (Cao and Wang, 1990), and fluorescently labeled myosin II (DeBiasio et al., 1996) all revealed concerted cortical flow towards the division plane in the equatorial region of the cell that contrasted with random surface movements at the cell poles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to prior work in vertebrate cells.

claim: Feedback in which relaxation enables compression-driven cortical flow may be a conserved feature of animal cell cytokinesis.
source: These observations suggest that feedback in which relaxation enables compression-driven cortical flow may be a conserved feature of animal cell cytokinesis.
evidence: This is proposed in the Discussion section based on observations in multiple systems.

claim: Following anaphase onset, contractile ring components are initially recruited to the equatorial cortex de novo, but then component levels are amplified by a feedback loop that involves flow and compression of cortical surface as well as de novo component loading.
source: In our model, following anaphase onset contractile ring components are initially recruited to the equatorial cortex de novo, as has been observed (Vale et al., 2009; Yumura, 2001; Zhou and Wang, 2008), but then component levels are amplified by a feedback loop that involves flow and compression of cortical surface as well as de novo component loading.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to prior work on de novo recruitment.

claim: Both de novo loading of components by Rho-based signaling and compression-driven flow contribute to the change in component levels in the ring during constriction.
source: Thus, in our model, both de novo loading of components by Rho-based signaling and compression-driven flow contribute to the change in component levels in the ring during constriction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a resolution to a debate in the field.

claim: The Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model provides a simple framework that can be used to analyze the consequences of molecular perturbations.
source: In addition to describing the processes underlying the evolution of the contractile ring, the Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model provides a simple framework that can be used to analyze the consequences of molecular perturbations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a utility of the model.

claim: Parameter changes derived from the model can be used as input for a finite-element model to predict the evolution of cell shape.
source: An additional interesting future direction will be to use parameter changes derived from the model as input for a finite-element model (similar to Turlier et al., 2014) in order to predict the evolution of cell shape given an a priori knowledge of cortical and contractile ring dynamics.
evidence: This is proposed in the Discussion section as a future direction with citation to prior modeling work.

claim: Contractile rings maintain a relatively constant overall closure rate despite their progressively decreasing perimeter.
source: Timely constriction relies on the conserved ability of contractile rings to maintain a relatively constant overall closure rate despite their progressively decreasing perimeter (Biron et al., 2004; Bourdages et al., 2014; Calvert et al., 2011; Carvalho et al., 2009; Ma et al., 2012; Mabuchi, 1994; Pelham and Chang, 2002; Zumdieck et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: RhoA is activated in an equatorial zone in response to signaling by the anaphase spindle.
source: RhoA is activated in an equatorial zone (the 'Rho zone') in response to signaling by the anaphase spindle (Green et al., 2012; Jordan and Canman, 2012; Piekny et al., 2005) and patterns the equatorial cortex by recruiting contractile ring components from the cytoplasm (Vale et al., 2009; Yumura, 2001; Zhou and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: RhoA patterns the equatorial cortex by recruiting contractile ring components from the cytoplasm.
source: RhoA is activated in an equatorial zone (the 'Rho zone') in response to signaling by the anaphase spindle (Green et al., 2012; Jordan and Canman, 2012; Piekny et al., 2005) and patterns the equatorial cortex by recruiting contractile ring components from the cytoplasm (Vale et al., 2009; Yumura, 2001; Zhou and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: RhoA activates Rho kinase, which promotes the assembly and recruitment of myosin II.
source: RhoA activates Rho kinase, which promotes the assembly and recruitment of myosin II (Matsumura et al., 2011) and the cytokinesis formin that assembles the long actin filaments that make up the ring (Otomo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The cytokinesis formin assembles the long actin filaments that make up the ring.
source: RhoA activates Rho kinase, which promotes the assembly and recruitment of myosin II (Matsumura et al., 2011) and the cytokinesis formin that assembles the long actin filaments that make up the ring (Otomo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Contractile rings contain membrane-associated septin filaments and the filament cross linker anillin.
source: Contractile rings also contain membrane-associated septin filaments (Bridges and Gladfelter, 2015) and the filament cross linker anillin (D'Avino, 2009; Piekny and Maddox, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The equatorial cortex is compressed along the pole-to-pole axis after initial patterning, leading to the alignment of actin filament bundles as the ring forms in C. elegans.
source: Recent work in the Caenorhabditis elegans embryo suggests that the equatorial cortex is compressed along the pole-to-pole axis after this initial patterning, leading to the alignment of actin filament bundles as the ring forms (Reymann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation to recent work.

claim: Ring constriction is thought to be coupled to the progressive disassembly of the ring.
source: Constriction is thought to be coupled to the progressive disassembly of the ring (i.e. loss of components in proportion to reduction in length; Carvalho et al., 2009; Murrell et al., 2015; Schroeder, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Ring constriction must complete within a short cell cycle window during mitotic exit.
source: Ring constriction must complete within a short cell cycle window during mitotic exit (Canman et al., 2000; Martineau et al., 1995; Straight et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Myosin is present in small puncta distributed over the entire cortex that flow together with actin filaments.
source: In addition to its RhoA-dependent enrichment in the contractile ring, myosin is present in small puncta, distributed over the entire cortex, that flow together with actin filaments (LifeAct::mKate2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), validating their utility as fiduciary marks for monitoring cortical movements.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The contractile ring closes asymmetrically within the division plane in C. elegans.
source: Because the contractile ring closes asymmetrically within the division plane (Maddox et al., 2007; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), cortical dynamics are not cylindrically symmetric.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to prior work and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The velocity of cortical flow was higher on the top of the embryo during the first half of cytokinesis when the furrow ingresses from the top.
source: As expected, based on the asymmetric closure of the contractile ring within the division plane, the velocity of cortical flow was higher on the top of the embryo during the first half of cytokinesis when the furrow ingresses from the top (Figure 1B, black traces) and became higher on the bottom of the embryo towards the end when the furrow ingresses from the bottom (Figure 1B, grey traces; Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: The velocity of cortical flow became higher on the bottom of the embryo towards the end of cytokinesis when the furrow ingresses from the bottom.
source: As expected, based on the asymmetric closure of the contractile ring within the division plane, the velocity of cortical flow was higher on the top of the embryo during the first half of cytokinesis when the furrow ingresses from the top (Figure 1B, black traces) and became higher on the bottom of the embryo towards the end when the furrow ingresses from the bottom (Figure 1B, grey traces; Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: Cutting the cortex parallel to the division plane using a laser reveals that the cortex is under tension during cytokinesis.
source: Cutting the cortex parallel to the division plane using a laser revealed that the cortex is under tension during cytokinesis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In control embryos, more cortex flowed in from the posterior side than from the anterior side, likely due to distinct mechanical properties downstream of the polarity machinery.
source: In control embryos, more cortex flowed in from the posterior side than from the anterior side, likely due to distinct mechanical properties downstream of the polarity machinery.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of cortical flow.

claim: Arp2/3 inhibition impairs the recruitment of PAR-2 to the posterior cortex and makes myosin and actin dynamics on the posterior cortex more similar to those in embryo anterior.
source: Prior work showed that Arp2/3 inhibition impairs the recruitment of PAR-2 to the posterior cortex and makes myosin and actin dynamics on the posterior cortex more similar to those in embryo anterior (Xiong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibiting the Arp2/3 complex by depleting ARX-2 abolished the difference between the anterior and posterior sides in cortical flow but did not change the difference between the total amount of cortex entering the division plane and the area of the plane.
source: Inhibiting the Arp2/3 complex by depleting ARX-2 abolished the difference between the two sides but did not change the difference between the total amount of cortex entering the division plane and the area of the plane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Video 3.

claim: The increase in the per-unit-length amounts of myosin and anillin began on the top of the ring, which ingresses first, and initiated later on the bottom, which ingresses after the constriction midpoint.
source: The increase in the per-unit-length amounts of myosin and anillin began on the top of the ring, which ingresses first, and initiated later on the bottom, which ingresses after the constriction midpoint (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: At the four-cell stage, the range of ring sizes between furrow formation and contact with the midzone is much smaller than at the one-cell stage.
source: However, distinguishing between constant and exponential dynamics at the four-cell stage is challenging because the range of ring perimeters between furrow formation (perimeter ~50 µm) and contact with the midzone, which alters ring properties (perimeter ~23 µm; Carvalho et al., 2009), is too limited (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: The four-cell data for myosin levels are well fit by the same exponential equation that describes myosin and anillin accumulation at the one-cell stage.
source: Although not sufficient to demonstrate exponential accumulation on their own, the four-cell data are well fit by the same exponential equation that describes myosin and anillin accumulation at the one-cell stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C, Figure 3C), consistent with the idea that contractile ring components accumulate via the same mechanism during both divisions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model fits the data for per-unit-length amounts of ring myosin and anillin and the rates of ring shrinkage and cortical compression significantly better than the Retention model.
source: Comparison of the fits to the data for the per-unit-length amounts of ring myosin and anillin and the rates of ring shrinkage and cortical compression for the two models (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) suggested that, whereas the Retention model could approximate the data, the Constriction-Coupled Disassembly with Compression Feedback model fit the data significantly better.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The per-unit-length amount of fluorescent myosin in the bleached rings was equivalent to the per-unit-length amount of myosin in control rings minus the per-unit-length amount of myosin in the ring at the time when it was bleached.
